title: Tailfin R&D Builds a Singular Peregrine Inspired by Pass Hunting
content:
Inspired by Japanese Pass Hunting from the 1980s, UK bag company Tailfin pinged its in-house R&D company to develop a modern rendition of the classic Japanese sport to be displayed at the brand’s Bespoked Osaka booth this weekend. Let’s check it out!

Archival photos via @niigata0252

Pass Hunting

Pass hunting began in the 1980s as a non-competitive cycling and mountaineering sport focused on finding, riding, or carrying a bicycle over mountain passes. Both the Japanese and the French perfected and documented this adventurous form of cycling. Finding inspiration from over forty years of Pass Hunting, Tailfin pinged its R&D department to reimagine what a modern Tailfin lineup would look like if it were used in a traditional Pass Hunting setup.

In-House R&D

Tailfin’s prototyping department, whose workshop sits right next to the kitchen at Tailfin HQ, principally exists to build prototypes for the R&D Division, the brand’s roster of ultra athletes, kitting out some of the best ultra riders in the world with bleeding-edge bikepacking tech and enabling a fast, iterative way of developing products. A couple of times a year, the department also takes on an R&D Kitchen project, with one goal in mind: to have fun and experiment.

These projects have no commercial target. They are about creative freedom and play: throwing aside restrictive thinking and looking at things in a different way. Some ideas might come out of them, but that is not the goal. It’s fun, energizing, and very unserious. Tailfin’s usual briefs lean towards lighter and faster. On this one, the team asked themselves what they would want to take, and the answer was extra time and extra luxuries: a trip built around the stops rather than the distance.

Tailfin Inspiration

The kit started with a film camera, in keeping with an analog approach. Theo, from Tailfin’s product department, designed a front bag to carry it, with a map pocket for a real paper map, included for the romance of it. Molly reimagined one pannier as an insulated cool bag for cold beers and a refrigerated picnic, and made a separate bag for a small espresso maker. Callum, Soft Goods Prototyper, redesigned the frame bag with flip-top closures in place of zips. It is divided vertically rather than horizontally, with access at the front so it can be used while riding.

The rest of the kit includes a sketchbook, watercolors and pencils, a fishing rod, a Helinox chair and a towel, but no swimming costume, in case a remote wild swimming spot turns up.

Singular Peregrine Built For Pass Hunting

The result is a British take on that tradition, built around the new Singular Peregrine Mk5. Singular founder Sam Alison launched the Peregrine in 2008, combining fat tires, drop bars and disc brakes on a classically styled lugged steel frame, and it was a gravel bike before the category had a name. The fifth generation keeps that character and refines it.

The British-designed frame is paired with a mix of British and Japanese components, and with Tailfin’s own versions of two touring classics: low front panniers and a randonneur handlebar bag. Both are made in British waxed canvas that weathers naturally, and both use the same mounting hardware and stability engineering as Tailfin’s race gear.

Making the aesthetic British gave the team another muse: a friend of the team and Bristol tailor David Darby Minns, who brought fabric samples and books full of vintage tailoring, old waxed jackets and pictures of fly fishing.

The setup is not a product in development, though Tailfin expects ideas from the project to inform future work.
